strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting: the heavy computational and memory burden of per-Gaussian neural deformation inference during both rendering and training.

Well-motivated and complementary technical contributions: Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) effectively extends static second-order sensitivity metrics across temporal frames; Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) introduces temporal perturbation to expose unstable primitives and suppress floaters; and GroupFlow achieves significant speedups by distilling per-primitive deformations into grouped SE(3) transformations.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The proposed framework is evaluated across 50 scenes on MonoDyGauBench spanning 5 distinct datasets (synthetic and real-world), with results averaged over three independent runs.

Significant practical gains: SpeeDe3DGS achieves up to 13.7x rendering acceleration, >2.5x training speedups, and an order of magnitude reduction in primitive count, substantially reducing memory consumption and allowing training on standard 24GB GPUs without significant quality degradation.
Thorough ablation studies exploring group count J, densification/post-densification pruning percentages, and individual component contributions.
weaknesses: Limitations on non-rigid motion fidelity: While GroupFlow provides substantial speedups, approximating deformation fields with piecewise rigid SE(3) clusters can lead to visual quality drops in scenes with strong non-rigid deformation or topological variation (e.g., PSNR drops from 23.55 to 21.00 on 4DGS in Table 2).

Continuous temporal interpolation and sequence length scalability: GroupFlow explicitly learns/stores SE(3) transformations per group across discrete frames. The paper does not thoroughly discuss how the representation scales to very long sequences or how continuous time interpolation is handled during novel view/time synthesis compared to continuous neural fields.

Incremental novelty for sensitivity pruning: The formulation of TSP closely follows static Hessian/gradient-based sensitivity pruning methods (Speedy-Splat and PUP 3D-GS), primarily extending the summation over timesteps.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck: dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models relying on neural deformation fields achieve strong visual quality but suffer from heavy per-Gaussian neural evaluation and slow rendering/training.

Technically coherent and well-motivated framework consisting of three complementary components: Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) to eliminate redundant primitives across space-time, Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) to identify and prune temporally unstable floaters via annealed temporal jittering, and GroupFlow to distill per-Gaussian continuous deformations into compact, shared rigid SE(3) cluster motions.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: the method is benchmarked across 50 scenes in MonoDyGauBench spanning 5 distinct datasets (NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, Nerfies, iPhone), with experiments repeated three times to report variance-reduced averages.

Impressive efficiency gains: delivers substantial speedups (up to 10×–29× rendering acceleration, reaching 250–500+ FPS), reduces primitive counts by over 10×, and cuts training time by over 2× with minimal loss in image quality metrics (and occasionally improved SSIM/LPIPS due to floater suppression).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: TSP is a direct temporal summation of the second-order gradient sensitivity metric from Speedy-Splat / PUP 3D-GS, and grouping motion via control points/rigid clusters builds upon concepts explored in prior work (e.g., SC-GS, SPGaussian), although the specific post-hoc Umeyama distillation design is practical and effective.

Multi-stage pipeline complexity: The training workflow involves soft pruning during densification, hard pruning post-densification, followed by trajectory clustering, Umeyama alignment initialization, and subsequent refinement of learnable SE(3) parameters. This introduces several empirical hyperparameters (e.g., cluster count J=2048, sampling limit N_max=100, weighting ratio lambda_r=0.5, pruning thresholds).

Fidelity degradation on highly complex or non-rigid deformations: When scenes feature intricate non-rigid deformations, approximating motion with rigid SE(3) clusters can lead to visible quality trade-offs (e.g., 4DGS + GroupFlow exhibits a ~2.5 dB PSNR drop on MonoDyGauBench, and D-NeRF PSNR drops by nearly 2 dB under DeformableGS + GroupFlow).

Minor inconsistencies and typos in experimental presentation: Table 15 mentions 'ASP' instead of 'TSP', and training time comparisons across Table 2 mix hardware (RTX 3090 vs. RTX A5000), which although both are 24GB Ampere cards, introduces slight architectural differences.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and practical bottleneck in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting: the heavy computational cost of per-Gaussian neural deformation inference during both training and real-time rendering.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The proposed framework is benchmarked across all 50 scenes in MonoDyGauBench spanning five datasets (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, NeRF-DS, Nerfies, iPhone), with experiments repeated over three runs to account for training variance.

Substantial empirical efficiency gains: SpeeDe3DGS reduces Gaussian primitive counts by ~10–12×, accelerates rendering up to 13–29× (achieving 270–500+ FPS), and speeds up training by ~2–3× while maintaining or slightly exceeding baseline visual quality (SSIM/MS-SSIM).

Thoughtful design of complementary components: Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) effectively addresses temporal floaters via jittered probing, and GroupFlow provides a practical neural-to-rigid distillation pipeline using trajectory clustering and Umeyama alignment.
Comprehensive ablation studies analyzing key hyperparameters, including the number of motion groups J and a 2D grid sweep over densification-stage and post-densification pruning ratios.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty of individual components: Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) is a relatively straightforward temporal aggregation extension of static sensitivity pruning (e.g., Speedy-Splat/PUP 3D-GS), while trajectory clustering into shared rigid SE(3) transformations shares conceptual similarities with existing group-based and skinning-based dynamic representations.

Performance degradation on complex non-rigid motion: While GroupFlow works well for scenes with predominantly locally rigid motion, its performance degrades noticeably on complex non-rigid deformation (e.g., when applied to 4DGS in Table 2, PSNR drops from 23.55 dB to 21.00 dB, and LPIPS increases from 0.277 to 0.380). A deeper discussion analyzing why 4DGS suffers significantly more under GroupFlow than DeformableGS is missing.

Storage scaling over long temporal sequences: GroupFlow explicitly parameterizes and stores rigid transformations {R_j^t, T_j^t} for every group j and every frame t. Table 1 indicates that adding GroupFlow increases model size from 4.55 MB to 21.40 MB. For sequences with thousands of frames, this per-frame group representation will scale linearly with time and lack continuous temporal interpolation/extrapolation.

Hardware heterogeneity across reported timing metrics: Training times in Tables 1, 2, and 15 are gathered across different GPU architectures (RTX 3090, RTX A5000, RTX A6000) due to baseline memory constraints. While noted in footnotes, this makes direct wall-clock comparisons less straightforward.
